claims.claim: The subject is the difference between joint, concurrent and simple resolutions
claims.sourceSpan: four forms of legislative measures may be introduced (or, in the case of resolutions, submitted) and acted on: bills, joint resolutions, concurrent resolutions, and resolutions of one house

claims.claim: Not everything Congress passes is a bill; the forms carry different legal weight
claims.sourceSpan: They are not lawmaking vehicles and are not submitted to the President for approval.

claims.claim: Same framing as the meta description
claims.sourceSpan: Concurrent resolutions are potentially considered in both chambers, but are also not presented to the President.

claims.claim: CRS statement of the lawmaking / internal-affairs division across the four forms
claims.sourceSpan: When Congress seeks to pass a law, it uses a bill or joint resolution, which must be passed by both houses in identical form and then presented to the President for the executive's approval or disapproval. To regulate its own internal affairs, or for other purposes where authority of law is not necessary, Congress uses a concurrent resolution (requiring adoption by both houses) or a simple resolution (requiring action only in the house of origin).

claims.claim: CRS: a concurrent resolution is not a law, so the President cannot sign or veto it, it has no statutory effect, no money can be raised or spent pursuant to it, and its purpose is to establish the framework for later budget measures
claims.sourceSpan: Because a concurrent resolution is not a law, the President cannot sign or veto it, and it does not have statutory effect, so no money can be raised or spent pursuant to it. REMOVED, U-FLAG and factually wrong: "This is one of the very few instances where a legislative measure that requires both-chamber agreement bypasses the President entirely." Concurrent resolutions also require both chambers and are also not presented to the President (CRS R42843 fn.7), so the amendment case is not rare in that respect. Replaced with the four-form presentment comparison drawn from R42843 fn.7 and R46603.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "The choice between the two is usually a matter of convention." CRS puts it as a difference of purpose, not convention - joint resolutions "may differ from bills in their purpose" - and the page now quotes the statutory form difference (1 U.S.C. 101 vs 102) plus CRS use-lists for each form instead of characterising the choice.

SOURCED, was U-FLAG (sweep found zero corpus hits for AUMF): "AUMFs are typically joint resolutions, given the temporal and contingent nature of the authority they grant." The unsourced rationale is gone; what remains is CRS R46603 own list entry, "declaration of war or authorization of military force," quoted as one of the uses of joint resolutions.

REMOVED from Key Sources and JSON-LD: the congress.gov legislative-glossary anchor link, which was one of only two citations on the page and was not the source of anything written here. The 5 U.S.C. 802 uscode.house.gov link already carried the &edition=prelim parameter and is kept; 1 U.S.C. 101/102, the Constitution transcript, R46603 and R42843 are added.

SOURCING DECISION: CRS 98-706 (Bills and Resolutions: Examples of How Each Kind Is Used) was fetched and stored for this batch and carries the same four use-lists, but its last revision is December 2, 2010. CRS R46603 is the current successor (last updated 2025-08-27) and R42843 (2025-11-19) supplies the presentment rules, so both lists on this page are drawn from the current products and 98-706 is NOT cited. This is the stale-secondary-source-as-current-rule class the batch was told to watch.

SOURCING NOTE: the stored R46603 capture carries CRS footnote numbers INLINE inside its use-lists (e.g. "regular annual general appropriations; 5 supplemental appropriations 6 ; reconciliation bills 7"). Quoting a whole list as one span would silently swallow those markers, which is an alteration inside quotation marks. Every list on this page is therefore quoted as SHORT separate fragments joined by punctuation outside the quotation marks, and each fragment is its own ledger row with its own receipt.

SOURCING NOTE: the stored R46603 capture renders "sine die" as "adjournment s ine die" (an italic-run artifact of the extraction). The page therefore states adjournment sine die OUTSIDE quotation marks; the ledger receipt records the mangled stored form so the row still resolves against the file.

BATCH-WIDE SWEEP (2026-09-02), the systemic defect of this batch: 104 instances across all seven articles where a comma, period, semicolon or colon sat INSIDE a closing quotation mark although the source has no such character at that point. American typographic convention puts them there; this site rule does not allow it, because a span in quotation marks is a promise of verbatimness and invented punctuation inside the marks breaks that promise for a reader checking the source. Two hostile passes had each flagged one or two instances individually, which produced iterative one-at-a-time fixes and, on one span, three successive wrong repairs. The class was instead resolved MECHANICALLY: a scanner extracted every quoted span on every page, tested it against the concatenated registered sources for that article, and where the span matched only after stripping one trailing punctuation character, moved that character outside the closing quote. Per-article counts: what-is-a-committee 32, discharge-petition 22, house-rules-committee 19, bill-numbering 12, congressional-oversight 8, how-to-read-a-bill 7, joint-resolution 4. A re-scan after the sweep returns zero. No word in any quotation changed; only the position of punctuation relative to the closing mark.

SWEEP FOLLOW-UP, adjudicated not fixed: after the punctuation sweep the scanner still flags a handful of spans per page. Every one was inspected. They fall into three groups, none a defect. (1) Nested-quote renderings, where the source own internal quotation marks arrive as HTML entities or as double-backtick/double-apostrophe pairs and the page renders them as single quotes so they can sit inside a double-quoted span - already adjudicated per-article in earlier rounds. (2) Scanner pairing artefacts, where an odd number of quote characters in a paragraph makes the scanner slice across a boundary and produce a span that was never on the page. (3) The literal string article-body, which is the class attribute the scanner picks up when it strips tags. Recorded so a future audit running the same scanner does not re-open them.
